html:
A Greek mathematician, engineer and inventor of Syracuse in Sicily, who lived from about 287 to 212 BCE. He is often ranked among the greatest mathematicians of all time.

His work included:

  • the area of a circle and the volume and surface of a sphere, found by a method close to later calculus. He was proudest of showing that a sphere has two thirds the volume of the cylinder around it.
  • a close estimate of pi, between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7.
  • the law of the lever, and the law of floating bodies, said to have come to him in the bath ("Eureka!").
  • the water-lifting screw named after him.

He wrote to scholars at Alexandria, heirs of Euclid. In the Second Punic War Syracuse sided with Carthage, and his war machines held off the Roman siege for two years. When the city fell in 212 BCE, a Roman soldier killed him, against the orders of the general Marcellus. Some of his work survived only in the Archimedes Palimpsest, scraped and written over as a prayer book in the 1200s.
